flashcards.q: How do Claude Code and Codex CLI differ at the protocol layer despite being architecturally close cousins?
flashcards.a: Claude Code's control plane sits on MCP for tools; Codex built a bespoke Item/Turn/Thread protocol over JSON-RPC/JSONL specifically because approval flows, streaming diffs, and thread persistence needed more expressiveness than a tool-oriented protocol gives.

flashcards.q: State the two benchmark results (as of 2026-08-01) that rank Claude Code and Codex oppositely, and why both can be true.
flashcards.a: Codex leads Terminal-Bench 2.0 (77.3% vs 65.4%, terminal/DevOps-weighted). Claude wins ~67% of blind pairwise reviews on code cleanliness/idiom/diff size. Different benchmarks measure different things -- a single ranking doesn't transfer across task types.

flashcards.q: Why is Cursor structurally, not just currently, unable to run headless in CI?
flashcards.a: Cursor is an IDE -- its entire interaction model assumes a human watching diffs in an editor. This is architectural, not a missing feature or settings gap that an update would close.

flashcards.q: What does Microsoft Agent Framework actually compete with -- is it a fourth finished coding agent?
flashcards.a: No. It's a harness-BUILDING SDK, one level down the stack from Claude Code/Codex/Cursor. It competes with hand-rolling your own harness, ships all 15 harness components opt-out rather than opt-in, and is positioned to carry forward investment in other frameworks.

flashcards.q: What is the documented Agent Framework gotcha for long sessions dying at the context limit?
flashcards.a: Compaction is silently disabled unless BOTH MaxContextWindowTokens and MaxOutputTokens are supplied -- a two-parameter config gap with no error, the most commonly reported 'why did my session die' cause in that framework.

flashcards.q: What is the specific headless-mode gotcha in Claude Code's permission system?
flashcards.a: PermissionRequest hooks (the interactive approval flow) do NOT fire in -p/headless mode. Enforcement must be re-derived via PreToolUse hooks or --allowedTools; interactive permission setup does not transfer to CI unchanged.

flashcards.q: Distinguish model lock-in from workflow/IDE lock-in, using Cursor as the example.
flashcards.a: Cursor's bring-your-own-API-key reduces MODEL lock-in (reach Claude, GPT, Gemini through one IDE) but creates real WORKFLOW lock-in (extensions, keybindings, muscle memory are Cursor-specific). Claude Code/Codex are the inverse: fully model-locked but lower workflow lock-in since a terminal prompt-in/diff-out pattern transfers more easily.

flashcards.q: How does Cursor's cost model differ structurally from Claude Code/Codex, and what's the visible lever?
flashcards.a: Cursor uses credit-metered pricing (shifted from request quotas in 2025, split into Composer/Auto vs Third-Party-API pools mid-2026); Max mode expands context up to 1M tokens at proportionally higher credit cost per request -- a cost lever a user pulls per-request rather than a fixed subscription.

flashcards.q: Give the two distinct kinds of 'control over the loop' and which tools offer which.
flashcards.a: Configuration control (hooks, permission rules -- Claude Code and Codex both give plenty) vs implementation control (rewriting compaction/permission/approval logic itself -- only Agent Framework or hand-rolling offer this).

flashcards.q: When is hand-rolling your own loop (no framework at all) the right call over all four options?
flashcards.a: When the task is narrow enough that a 15-component harness is negative value (a 3-10 step loop, one model, fixed small tool set is ~40 lines), or when requirements are unusual enough that even Agent Framework's flexibility doesn't fit.

flashcards.q: A team needs to audit every tool call against a compliance policy service. Which of the four tools fits, and why do the other three fail?
flashcards.a: Agent Framework -- it requires implementation control over the permission engine (an external policy-service call per tool call), which none of the three finished products expose as an extension point beyond fixed hooks or diff-accept UIs.

flashcards.q: Why should hard requirements (like headless CI) be treated as disqualifying rather than averaged with other axes when scoring these tools?
flashcards.a: A tool excellent on 8 axes that structurally cannot meet a required 9th (e.g. Cursor + headless CI) is disqualified, not '8/9 good.' Averaging hides an architectural gap that will surface later as a costly tool-switch.

flashcards.q: Why does this module explicitly flag its own benchmark numbers as having a short shelf life?
flashcards.a: Four vendors ship monthly; any specific score is a snapshot, not a durable fact. The axes (loop control, context mgmt, permission granularity, headless usability, cost, lock-in) are stable evaluation dimensions -- the numbers on them are not.

flashcards.q: What is the most common real-world tool combination reported for these four options?
flashcards.a: Cursor + Claude Code stacked together -- Cursor for in-editor, human-supervised work; Claude Code for terminal-heavy, headless, or long-running tasks -- treated as complementary rather than an either/or choice.

flashcards.q: Does choosing the 'best' harness substitute for review discipline?
flashcards.a: No. Harness choice changes how fast and cleanly code gets generated, not whether the resulting architecture and review process are sound. Weak review discipline produces bad outcomes on all four tools, just at different speeds.
